History:
- Presenting complaint: 2–3 days of exertional shortness of breath with wheeze and cough.
- Onset/duration/progression: Symptoms began 2–3 days ago during running; now occur with brisk walking and at times at rest. Blue reliever inhaler used with little benefit.
- Associated symptoms: Wheezing and coughing. No sputum production reported.
- Triggers/context: Symptoms provoked by exercise; patient usually able to talk while running previously. No recent hospital admissions.
- Previous episodes: Last notable asthma attack ~3–4 years ago. Asthma was generally controlled until current episode.
- Self-monitoring: Peak flow when well ~380 L/min; no recent peak flow recorded since symptoms began.
- Recent care: Last asthma review ~2 years ago.

Past Medical History:
- Asthma (on inhaled therapy; details below).
- Possible eczema (patient reports skin issues that may be eczema).
- Allergic rhinitis/hay fever.
- No known drug allergies reported.
- Hospitalizations: None reported for asthma.
- Oral steroids: Patient reports no prior oral steroid courses (conflict: clinician indicated possible steroid need if exam abnormal).
- Current medications reported by patient:
  - Salbutamol (blue inhaler) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Clenil (brown inhaler; inhaled corticosteroid preventive) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Cetraben — dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Hydrocortisone — dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - (Patient initially mentioned “Flanel Bactroban” then later “Cetraben”; see conflicts below.)

Physical Examination:
- No formal examination recorded in transcript.
- Patient-reported findings: audible wheeze and shortness of breath; no sputum.
- Mental status: Alert and conversational during consult.
- No throat swelling or other acute features documented.

Impression:
- Likely mild asthma exacerbation (exercise-induced/worsening control) over last 2–3 days.

Management Plan:
- Arrange face-to-face GP review within the next few days for chest examination and peak flow measurement.
- Interim self-management advised:
  - Continue blue reliever (salbutamol) as needed; may use up to every 2–4 hours if symptomatic (use frequently indicates poor control and need for urgent review).
  - Increase inhaled corticosteroid (Clenil) to 4 puffs twice daily while awaiting review (current dose not documented; instruction given by clinician).
- If breathing substantially worsens or patient deteriorates before review: attend A&E urgently rather than wait for appointment.
- Possible additional treatments at face-to-face visit depending on exam/peak flow: oral steroids and/or antibiotics if clinically indicated.

Patient Summary:
- Patient with known asthma developed increased exertional breathlessness, wheeze, and cough over 2–3 days unresponsive to usual blue inhaler. Clinician suspects a mild exacerbation and advised interim escalation of inhaled steroid and regular reliever use, with prompt face-to-face GP review and instruction to go to A&E if symptoms worsen.

Key Takeaways:
- Use salbutamol (blue inhaler) as needed, up to every 2–4 hours if symptomatic.
- Increase Clenil (brown inhaler) to 4 puffs twice daily while awaiting review.
- If breathing becomes much worse, present to A&E immediately.

Next Steps:
- Booked/arranged: face-to-face GP appointment within a few days for chest exam and peak flow.
- At that visit: clinical assessment may prompt oral steroids and/or antibiotics based on findings.
- Patient to monitor symptoms and peak flow if possible and seek emergency care for deterioration.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: current vital signs (respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, heart rate), current peak flow reading during this episode, exact doses/routes/frequencies for all inhalers and topical medications, smoking status, pregnancy status (if relevant), full medication reconciliation, and contact/follow-up scheduling details.
- Internal conflicts from transcript:
  - Patient initially listed medications as “Salbutamol, Flanel Bactroban and Hydrocortisone” and later as “Cetraben and Hydrocortisone” — conflict noted regarding topical medication names.
  - Patient initially stated preventer was “blue,” but clinician referred to the brown inhaler (Clenil) as the preventer; conflict noted about which inhaler is the preventer.
- Transcript quality comment: Mostly intelligible but contains some brief unclear phrases and repetitions; medication names and some details required clarification during the encounter.
